answer.evidence: The trained first-layer units fall into two mirror-image families; the rest (0,1,5,6,9-13,15,16,20,23,31) have small, unstructured weights that look like untrained noise. Family B (units 3,7,8,21,22,24,27,28) has strong positive weights on an annulus (rows ~5-18, cols ~5-18) and negative weights on the central ~4x4 core (rows 10-13, cols 10-13). These units feed layer-2 units u0, u1, u7, u8 and u15, which have positive output weights, so they push toward class 1 (large). Family A (units 2,4,14,17,18,19,25,26,29,30) is the opposite: large positive biases, a positive centre, a negative annulus and a broadly positive periphery. They feed u9 and u11 (output weights -86 and -73), so they push toward class 0 (small). Both families are roughly symmetric top/bottom and left/right. Neither has a compact, consistently strong off-blob patch such as a corner or edge marker. Some isolated pixels (e.g. r1 c16-17, r23 c7, r23 c11, r8 c2) carry consistent opposite signs across the two families. These are scattered single pixels rather than a coherent region, consistent with fitting background noise in a finite dataset. The broad positive periphery in Family A is uniform, so it acts like a bias drift from mean background intensity rather than a localized cue.
answer.main_feature: The model compares brightness in a ring at radius ~3-8 px around the centre with brightness in the central core. Bright ring pixels (blob extends outward) activate the large-blob family, and a bright core with a dark ring activates the small-blob family.
